1.summary: Nahum opens with a hymn to Yahweh as the jealous, avenging God who is also a refuge for those who trust him, and then announces that Assyria's yoke on Judah will be broken.
1.lookfor: Notice how the hymn describes God's power over nature, the verse that interrupts the wrath in 1:7, and the messenger on the mountains at the end.

names.name: Nineveh
names.gloss: The capital of Assyria on the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul in Iraq.

names.name: Nahum
names.gloss: The prophet; his name means comfort.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: Fertile land east of the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Carmel
names.gloss: A green ridge on Israel's northern coast.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains to the north, famous for forests and flowers.

insights.title: Assyria's long shadow
insights.body: For over a century Assyria had dominated the Near East. It destroyed Samaria in 722 BC, devastated Judah in 701 BC, and made its kings pay tribute. Its own royal inscriptions boast of flaying, impaling and deporting conquered peoples. Nahum speaks to those who had suffered under it.

insights.title: Slow to anger, but
insights.body: Yahweh is slow to anger ... and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished (1:3) reworks God's self-description from Exodus 34. Jonah dwells on God's mercy toward Nineveh; Nahum, drawing on the same words, stresses God's justice toward it. Together the two books show both sides of the same creed.

insights.title: A jealous God
insights.body: The opening calls Yahweh a jealous God who avenges (1:2). In Hebrew, jealous, qanna, describes passionate commitment to his people and his honour, like a spouse's protective love. Vengeance here means God setting things right for victims, not personal spite.

insights.title: A broken acrostic
insights.body: In Hebrew, verses 2-8 seem to follow the alphabet, with lines beginning with successive letters from aleph to about kaph. The pattern is incomplete and disputed. Other acrostics appear in the Psalms and Lamentations.

insights.title: A stronghold in trouble
insights.body: In the middle of the storm of wrath stands a quiet verse: Yahweh is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him (1:7). The same power that terrifies enemies protects those who trust him. Knows means cares for, as in a covenant relationship.

insights.title: Breaking the yoke
insights.body: I will break his yoke from off you (1:13) promises Judah freedom from Assyrian vassalage. Assyrian treaties bound vassal kings with oaths and tribute, and rebels were savagely punished. Judah's King Manasseh spent most of his reign as an Assyrian vassal.

insights.title: Feet on the mountains
insights.body: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! (1:15) is nearly identical to Isaiah 52:7. In Nahum the good news is Nineveh's fall; Isaiah's is return from exile. Paul quotes the line about those who preach the gospel. In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 2:1.

insights.title: Comfort through judgment
insights.body: Nahum's name means comfort, yet his book is about destruction. For people crushed by an empire, its fall was good news. Can God's judgment on oppressors itself be a form of comfort to the oppressed?

2.summary: Nahum vividly describes the attack on Nineveh: chariots rushing through the streets, the river gates opened, the palace collapsing, the city plundered, and the lions' den emptied.
2.lookfor: Notice the pace of the battle scene, the role of water, and the extended picture of Assyria as a lion.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: A name for God's people, descended from Jacob.

insights.title: The fall of Nineveh
insights.body: In 612 BC a coalition of Babylonians and Medes besieged and destroyed Nineveh. The Babylonian Chronicle records its capture after about three months. The Assyrian empire collapsed within a few years, and Nineveh was never rebuilt as a great city.

insights.title: Red shields
insights.body: The shields of the attackers are red and the soldiers wear scarlet (2:3). Shields may have been covered with red-dyed leather, and Ezekiel describes Babylonian officers portrayed in vermilion. The flash of chariots like torches and lightning (2:4) gives the scene a cinematic speed.

insights.title: The gates of the rivers
insights.body: The gates of the rivers are opened, and the palace is dissolved (2:6). Nineveh lay on the Tigris with the Khosr river running through it, controlled by dams and sluice gates. The Greek historian Diodorus later wrote that a flood broke down part of the walls, and some think the attackers used the water system against the city.

insights.title: Like a pool of water
insights.body: Nineveh has been like a pool of water (2:8), full and calm, but now its people drain away. Stop! Stop! they cry, but no one turns back. The city that gathered the wealth of nations empties out in panic.

insights.title: Plunder
insights.body: Take the plunder of silver; take the plunder of gold (2:9). Nineveh held tribute from across the empire. Assyrian reliefs often show soldiers carrying away the treasures of conquered cities; now it is Nineveh's turn.

insights.title: The empty lions' den
insights.body: Where is the den of the lions? (2:11). Assyrian kings portrayed themselves as lions and hunted lions in staged royal hunts, famously carved on Ashurbanipal's palace walls. Nahum pictures Assyria as a lion that tore prey for its cubs, now with its den empty.

insights.title: I am against you
insights.body: Behold, I am against you, says Yahweh of Armies (2:13). Behind the armies of Babylon and Media, Nahum sees Yahweh himself. The voice of Assyria's messengers, who once delivered threats to Jerusalem, will be silenced.

insights.title: Joy at a city's fall
insights.body: The chapter describes terror and suffering in Nineveh with something like satisfaction. Readers have found this troubling, and some Christian and Jewish interpreters stress that the book celebrates the end of oppression rather than suffering itself. How should God's people respond when a cruel power falls?

3.summary: Nahum pronounces woe on Nineveh, the bloody city full of lies and plunder, compares it with Thebes, which also fell, and mocks its useless defences and officials before ending with its fatal wound.
3.lookfor: Notice the rapid images of battle in 3:2-3, the comparison with No-Amon, and the question that ends the book.

names.name: No-Amon
names.gloss: Thebes, the great city of Upper Egypt on the Nile, sacked by Assyria in 663 BC.

names.name: Cush
names.gloss: The land south of Egypt along the Nile; its kings ruled Egypt for a time.

names.name: Put
names.gloss: A people of Africa, perhaps in Libya.

names.name: Assyria
names.gloss: The empire whose capital was Nineveh.

insights.title: The bloody city
insights.body: Woe to the bloody city! (3:1). Assyrian kings boasted in their inscriptions of piling up heads, flaying rebels and impaling them on stakes, and palace reliefs depicted such scenes. Nahum's charge is that Nineveh built its wealth on violence and lies.

insights.title: Sound and fury
insights.body: The cracking whip, rattling wheels, galloping horses and flashing swords (3:2-3) are described in short bursts that mimic the speed of battle. The scene ends with heaps of corpses that the soldiers stumble over. Nahum is among the most vivid poets of the Old Testament.

insights.title: A troubling image
insights.body: God threatens to lift Nineveh's skirts and expose her (3:5), using the image of a prostitute publicly shamed. Ancient prophets used such language for conquered cities, and modern readers rightly find it disturbing. Its point is that Nineveh's seductive power, which sold nations (3:4), will be exposed for what it is.

insights.title: Thebes fell too
insights.body: Are you better than No-Amon? (3:8). Thebes in Upper Egypt, defended by the Nile and allied with Cush and Libya, was sacked by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in 663 BC. Nahum turns Assyria's own conquest into a warning: if Thebes could fall, so can Nineveh.

insights.title: Ripe figs
insights.body: Nineveh's fortresses are like ripe figs that fall into the mouth of the eater when the tree is shaken (3:12). Its troops are like women, an ancient insult for soldiers without courage (3:13). Its defences will collapse at the first touch.

insights.title: Locusts fly away
insights.body: Nineveh's merchants and officials are like locusts that settle on walls in the cold but fly away when the sun appears (3:16-17). Its bureaucracy and trade network will vanish when the heat comes. The image mocks an empire that seemed everywhere.

insights.title: Who has not felt your cruelty?
insights.body: The book ends with a question: who hasn't felt your endless cruelty? (3:19). Jonah also ends with a question about Nineveh: should God not be concerned for it? Read together, the two books raise the question of how God's patience and justice relate.

insights.title: Clapping hands
insights.body: All who hear the news clap their hands (3:19). The world rejoices at the fall of an oppressor. Revelation later uses the fall of Babylon in similar terms to picture the end of every empire built on violence.

intro.who: Nahum the Elkoshite, whose name means comfort; nothing else is known of him, and the location of Elkosh is uncertain. Traditions place it in Galilee, in Judah, or near Nineveh itself.
intro.when: The book refers to the fall of Thebes in Egypt in 663 BC as past and looks ahead to the fall of Nineveh, which happened in 612 BC, so it is usually dated between those years, often near the end of the period.
intro.why: It announces the downfall of Nineveh, capital of the cruel Assyrian empire that had crushed Israel and dominated Judah, as Yahweh's just judgment and as comfort and good news for his oppressed people.
